cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Literature ≠ triviality – written works, especially those considered of superior or lasting artistic merit.

p.em: Example: Reading classic literature expands emotional understanding.

cosy-blockquote.p: Fiction ≠ fact – literature in the form of prose, especially short stories and novels, describing imaginary events.

p.em: Example: Fiction allows readers to inhabit different lives.

cosy-blockquote.p: Decline ≠ growth – a gradual and continuous loss of strength, numbers, quality, or value.

p.em: Example: Statistics show a decline in male fiction readers.

cosy-blockquote.p: Empathy ≠ indifference – the ability to understand and share the feelings of another.

p.em: Example: Reading novels builds deep interpersonal empathy.

cosy-blockquote.p: Narrative ≠ list – a spoken or written account of connected events; a story.

p.em: Example: A compelling narrative engages both heart and intellect.

cosy-blockquote.p: Insight ≠ ignorance – the capacity to gain an accurate and deep intuitive understanding of a person or thing.

p.em: Example: Great books offer profound psychological insight.

cosy-blockquote.p: Habit ≠ anomaly – a settled or regular tendency or practice.

p.em: Example: Daily reading habits have shifted toward short videos.

cosy-blockquote.p: Engagement ≠ distraction – the state of being involved and focused.

p.em: Example: Deep narrative engagement requires sustained attention.

cosy-blockquote.p: Perspective ≠ bias – a particular attitude toward or way of regarding something; a point of view.

p.em: Example: Literature exposes us to diverse cultural perspectives.

cosy-blockquote.p: Reflection ≠ impulse – serious thought or consideration.

p.em: Example: Reading requires quiet time for personal reflection.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Why has classical literature lost popularity among younger demographic groups?
★ What classic book made a deep impression on you in school?

How does reading immersive fiction expand emotional vocabulary and human empathy?
★ Do you prefer fiction novels or non-fiction biographies?

What factors account for the gradual decline in long-form reading habits worldwide?
★ Have your own reading habits changed over the past five years?

How does literary engagement cultivate deep interpersonal empathy in readers?
★ Do you feel connected to fictional characters in books?

What makes a compelling multi-generational narrative memorable across centuries?
★ What is your favorite story arc in literature or cinema?

How does deep reading provide unique psychological insight into human motivation?
★ Has a book ever changed your perspective on a major life issue?

Why is building a consistent daily reading habit challenging in the smartphone era?
★ Do you set aside dedicated time for reading every day?

What distinguishes intellectual engagement with text from passive video consumption?
★ Do you take notes or highlight passages when reading books?

How does literature offer a broader cultural perspective on historical events?
★ Do you enjoy reading books set in different cultures or eras?

Why is quiet time for personal reflection essential after finishing a great book?
★ Do you write book reviews or journal about what you read?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: A comparative reflection on our habits and self-perceptions.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Look at the prompt and discuss your response with your teacher:

cosy-blockquote.p: A comparative reflection on our habits and self-perceptions.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
The decline of literature reading among men threatens intellectual diversity. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Have you noticed fewer men reading fiction books today?

Reading complex fiction should be promoted as a vital mental health exercise. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Does reading fiction help you de-stress?

Reversing the global decline in book reading requires redesigning school curriculums. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ How should schools make literature exciting for kids?

Developing deep empathy through literature makes people better leaders and partners. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do well-read people make more empathetic friends?

A powerful written narrative has more impact on society than a documentary film. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Has a novel ever moved you more than a movie?

Gaining profound psychological insight requires reading books outside your comfort zone. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you read challenging or uncomfortable books?

Establishing a daily reading habit is more beneficial for focus than meditation. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Recommend reading as a daily mental discipline?

Active mental engagement with literature prevents cognitive decline in older age. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Believe reading keeps the mind young?

Gaining a multi-cultural perspective through literature reduces social prejudice. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Has literature broadened your worldview?

Making time for solitary reflection is essential in a fast-paced digital world. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you carve out quiet reflective time weekly?

ul.li: Incorrect: Men are reading less books since ten years. → Correct: Men have been reading fewer books for ten years. ((Use present perfect continuous + 'for' for duration up to present.))
Incorrect: Fiction books gives us empathies. → Correct: Fiction books give us empathy. ((Empathy is an uncountable abstract noun: use 'empathy'.))
